claim: Gene expression varies across genetically identical cells in homogeneous environments due to thermodynamic fluctuations in molecular events underlying gene expression and small numbers of molecules involved.
source: Many studies over the last decade have established that, even within homogeneous environments, gene expression varies across genetically identical cells due to thermodynamic fluctuations in the molecular events underlying gene expression and the small numbers of molecules involved (Elowitz et al., 2002; Rao et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to Elowitz et al., 2002 and Rao et al., 2002

claim: Most genes exhibit much larger fluctuations in their mRNA copy number than Poissonian fluctuations.
source: Although such Poissonian fluctuations are observed for some genes, most genes exhibit much larger fluctuations in their mRNA copy number.
evidence: Draws from established scientific understanding of gene expression noise

claim: Increased variability in mRNA copy number originates from promoters stochastically switching between different states associated with different transcription initiation rates.
source: It is generally believed that such increased variability originates in promoters stochastically switching between different states that are associated with different transcription initiation rates.
evidence: Represents established scientific consensus in the field

claim: Different promoters show different amounts of gene expression noise that are encoded in the promoter sequence.
source: Indeed, several studies have shown that different promoters show different amounts of gene expression noise, and that these differences are, at least to some extent, encoded in the promoter sequence (Newman et al., 2006; Hornung et al., 2012; Silander et al., 2012; Carey et al., 2013; Jones, et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous studies

claim: Several studies have provided evidence that selection generally acts to minimize noise.
source: Indeed, by investigating the association between expression noise and various statistics that can be considered proxies of organismal fitness, several studies have provided evidence that selection generally acts to minimize noise (Newman et al., 2006; Barkai and Shilo, 2007; Lehner, 2010; Lehner, 2008; Silander et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple previous studies

claim: Phenotypic diversity generated by gene expression noise can be selected for in fluctuating environments.
source: On the other hand, gene expression noise generates phenotypic diversity between organisms with identical genotypes, and there are well-established theoretical models showing that such phenotypic diversity can be selected for in fluctuating environments (Bull, 1987; Kussell and Leibler, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical models

claim: A large set of synthetic E. coli promoters was evolved de novo in the laboratory using an experimental protocol selecting on mean expression level with virtually no selection on noise properties.
source: To address this, we evolved a large set of synthetic Escherichia coli promoters de novo in the laboratory using an experimental protocol in which promoter sequences were selected on the basis of the mean expression level they conferred, while experiencing virtually no selection on their noise properties (Figure 1).
evidence: Describes the experimental design and methodology used in the study

claim: The initial library contained more than 1 million random promoter clones.
source: Beginning with a library of more than 1 million random promoter clones, we used fluorescence activated cell sorting (FACS) to select cells expressing specific levels of GFP (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: Describes the experimental setup

claim: 479 synthetic promoters were selected from the third and fifth rounds of FACS selection.
source: We selected a subset of 479 synthetic promoters from the third and fifth rounds of FACS selection, choosing equal numbers of promoters from each of six replicate lineages we evolved (Figure 1; 'Materials and methods').
evidence: Describes the experimental data collection

claim: Mean fluorescence levels were directly proportional to GFP molecule numbers.
source: We used quantitative Western blotting to confirm that the mean fluorescence levels were directly proportional to GFP molecule numbers (Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Appendix 1), which allowed us to express fluorescence levels in units of numbers of GFP molecules.
evidence: Confirmed by quantitative Western blotting experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: Fluorescence distributions across cells were well approximated by log-normal distributions.
source: Observing that the fluorescence distributions across cells were well approximated by log-normal distributions (Figure 1C), we characterized each promoter's distribution by the mean and variance of log-fluorescence, defining the latter as the promoter's noise level (Figure 1D).
evidence: Observed in experimental data shown in Figure 1C

claim: Differences in noise levels of the reporters are likely dominated by differences in transcriptional noise of the promoters.
source: Although our reporter constructs measure protein levels, that is, GFP, the differences in the noise levels of the reporters are likely dominated by differences in transcriptional noise of the promoters.
evidence: Based on logical inference from the experimental design where only promoter sequences differ

claim: Protein levels were determined primarily by mRNA levels.
source: Using qPCR we confirmed that protein levels were determined primarily by mRNA levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 3 and Appendix 1).
evidence: Confirmed by qPCR experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3

claim: Noise levels were reproducible across biological replicates.
source: Finally, we note that noise levels were reproducible across biological replicates (Figure 1—figure supplement 4), and noise levels estimated using microscopy were consistent with those measured by flow cytometry (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Demonstrated by replicate measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4

claim: A systematic relationship exists between the mean and variance of expression levels of each promoter.
source: Indeed, as expected (Bar-Even et al., 2006; Newman et al., 2006), we observed a systematic relationship between the mean and variance of expression levels of each promoter (Figure 1D).
evidence: Observed in experimental data shown in Figure 1D and supported by citations

claim: A strict lower bound on variance as a function of mean expression was observed.
source: In particular, we observed a strict lower bound on variance as a function of mean expression.
evidence: Observed in experimental data shown in Figure 1D

claim: Most synthetic promoters exhibited noise levels close to the minimal level exhibited by native promoters.
source: We found, surprisingly, that most of the synthetic promoters exhibited noise levels close to the minimal level exhibited by the native promoters (Figure 1D).
evidence: Observed in experimental data shown in Figure 1D

claim: A substantial fraction of native promoters exhibited excess noise levels significantly greater than the synthetic promoters.
source: Additionally, a substantial fraction of native promoters exhibited excess noise levels significantly greater than the synthetic promoters (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplements 6, 7).
evidence: Observed in experimental data shown in Figure 1E and supplementary figures

claim: Only 26.1% of synthetic promoters exhibited excess noise above 0.05, compared to 41.6% of native E. coli promoters.
source: For example, only 26.1% of the synthetic promoters exhibited excess noise above 0.05, compared to 41.6% of the native E. coli promoters (p < 7.7 × 10−10, hypergeometric test).
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data with p-value

claim: Functional E. coli promoters should exhibit low excess noise levels by default.
source: Given that the synthetic promoters were evolved from random sequence fragments and had not been selected on their noise properties (Appendix 2), we concluded that functional E. coli promoters should exhibit low excess noise levels by default.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental observations and selection protocol

claim: Native promoters with elevated excess noise must have experienced selective pressures that caused them to increase their noise.
source: Importantly, this implies that the native promoters with elevated excess noise must have experienced selective pressures that caused them to increase their noise.
evidence: Logical inference from the observation that synthetic promoters have low noise by default

claim: Promoters with high noise tend to show high expression plasticity.
source: Previous studies in Saccharomyces cerevisiae have shown that promoters with high noise tend to also show high expression plasticity, that is, large changes in mean expression level across environments (Newman et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Newman et al., 2006

claim: A significant association between expression plasticity and noise was confirmed in the present data.
source: Although we did not clearly observe this association in data from our previous study (Silander et al., 2012), a recent re-analysis of this data did uncover a significant association between expression plasticity and noise (Singh, 2013), which we confirmed using our present data (Figure 2A).
evidence: Confirmed by analysis of current experimental data shown in Figure 2A

claim: There is an equally strong relationship between excess noise and the number of regulators known to target the promoter.
source: In addition, we found that there is an equally strong relationship between excess noise and the number of regulators known to target the promoter (Salgado et al., 2013) (Figure 2B).
evidence: Observed in analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Excess noise levels of promoters without known regulatory inputs are very similar to those of synthetic promoters.
source: In particular, whereas the excess noise levels of promoters without known regulatory inputs are very similar to those of our synthetic promoters, promoters with one or more regulatory inputs have clearly elevated noise levels (Figure 2C).
evidence: Observed in experimental data shown in Figure 2C

claim: The general association between elevated noise and gene regulation has recently been observed in eukaryotes as well.
source: The general association between elevated noise and gene regulation has recently been observed in eukaryotes as well (Sharon et al., 2014), and mutations that lower gene expression noise typically target TF binding sites (Hornung et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sharon et al., 2014 and Hornung et al., 2012

claim: Any regulator will have some noise in its expression or activity, and this noise will be propagated to its target genes.
source: Indeed, any regulator will have some noise in its expression or activity, and this noise will be propagated to its target genes.
evidence: Based on established understanding of regulatory systems

claim: Noise-propagation causes an increase in expression noise of the targets.
source: Consequently, this 'noise-propagation' effect will cause an increase in expression noise of the targets (Thattai and van Oudenaarden, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Thattai and van Oudenaarden, 2001

claim: Under relatively mild assumptions, the fitness effects of a new regulatory interaction can be calculated analytically and depend on only a few effective parameters.
source: As explained in 'Materials and methods' and Appendix 3, we derive that, under relatively mild assumptions, the fitness effects of a new regulatory interaction can be calculated analytically, and depend on only a few effective parameters.
evidence: Derived from theoretical modeling described in Materials and methods and Appendix 3

claim: This equation applies independent of how the desired levels and regulator levels vary across environments and only depends on the assumption that the fitness function and expression distributions can be approximated by Gaussians.
source: Notably, this equation applies independent of how the desired levels μe and regulator levels re vary across the environments and only depends on the assumption that the fitness function and expression distributions can be approximated by Gaussians.
evidence: Stated as a property of the theoretical model

claim: Coupling to an uncorrelated noisy regulator substantially increases fitness.
source: Interestingly, coupling to a noisy regulator whose activity is entirely uncorrelated with the desired expression levels (blue dot in Figure 3B and Figure 3E,H) also substantially increases fitness.
evidence: Demonstrated by theoretical model shown in Figure 3

claim: In the regime where coupling to an uncorrelated noisy regulator increases fitness, the increased fitness results exclusively from the noise-propagation mechanism.
source: In this regime, the increased fitness results exclusively from the noise-propagation mechanism, and by coupling to the regulator the promoter effectively implements a bet hedging strategy.
evidence: Derived from theoretical model analysis

claim: Coupling to an uncorrelated noisy regulator can outperform coupling to a moderately correlated regulator.
source: Surprisingly, coupling to the uncorrelated noisy regulator (blue dot in Figure 3B and Figure 3E,H) outperforms coupling to a moderately correlated regulator (magenta dot in Figure 3B and Figure 3D,G).
evidence: Demonstrated by theoretical model shown in Figure 3

claim: Regulators may generally be under selection to become noisy themselves.
source: This illustrates that regulators may generally be under selection to become noisy themselves.
evidence: Inferred from theoretical model predictions

claim: There exists a continuum of regulatory strategies in which the condition-response and noise-propagation effects are optimally acting in concert.
source: Most interestingly, the red curve corresponds to a continuum of regulatory strategies in which the condition-response and noise-propagation effects are optimally acting in concert, going from being dominated by noise-propagation in the lower left, to being dominated by the condition-response in the top right.
evidence: Derived from theoretical model analysis

claim: Accurate regulation can evolve smoothly from a state without regulation by starting from coupling to a noisy regulator with low R and S, then increasing both R and S in incremental steps.
source: Importantly, this clarifies how accurate regulation can evolve smoothly from a state without regulation. Highly accurate regulation with high R and S can be reached by starting from coupling to a noisy regulator with low R and S, whose benefits come entirely from the noise-propagation, and then increasing both R and S in incremental steps along this continuum of regulatory strategies.
evidence: Inferred from theoretical model predictions

claim: The selective pressure for a promoter to evolve regulatory interactions is determined by the expression mismatch Y.
source: First, our model predicts that the selective pressure for a promoter to evolve regulatory interactions is determined by the expression mismatch Y.
evidence: Prediction from theoretical model

claim: When Y < 1, there will be no selective pressure to evolve regulation.
source: When Y < 1, even a constitutively expressed promoter has a good overlap with the fitness function across all conditions, and there will be no selective pressure to evolve regulation.
evidence: Prediction from theoretical model

claim: Constitutive promoters have low noise by default.
source: Our synthetic promoters, which were selected for expressing at a constant level, correspond to this situation, and our results show that such promoters have low noise by default. Thus, we interpret the observation that native promoters without known regulatory inputs have noise levels similar to those of our synthetic promoters (Figure 2B) as indicating that constitutive promoters have low noise by default.
evidence: Inferred from experimental observations and theoretical model

claim: The model predicts that expression plasticity and noise level should be correlated.
source: Our model thus predicts that the expression plasticity and noise level should be correlated.
evidence: Prediction from theoretical model

claim: The model predicts a general positive correlation between expression noise and the number of regulatory inputs.
source: Our model also predicts a general positive correlation between expression noise and the number of regulatory inputs.
evidence: Prediction from theoretical model

claim: The higher the initial mismatch Y, the larger the expected number of regulatory interactions necessary to reduce the mismatch below 1.
source: In this way, the higher the initial mismatch Y, the larger the expected number of regulatory interactions that will be necessary to reduce the mismatch below 1; that is, our model generally predicts that the number of regulatory interactions, the expression plasticity, and the final noise all correlate with the original mismatch Y.
evidence: Prediction from theoretical model

claim: In a given condition, the noise level of a promoter is determined by the noise levels of the TFs that regulate it.
source: More specifically, our model predicts that, in a given condition, the noise level of a promoter is determined by the noise levels of the TFs that regulate it.
evidence: Prediction from theoretical model

claim: A simple linear model assuming excess noise equals the sum of noise levels of regulating TFs explained 17% of the variance in excess noise levels across promoters.
source: To test this prediction, we used a very simple linear model that assumes that the excess noise level of a gene is equal to the sum of the noise levels of the TFs that regulate it ('Materials and methods'). Although this simple model is very crude, that is, assuming noise-propagation to be of equal size for all targets of a given TF, and assuming that fluctuations in TF activities are all independent, it was nevertheless able to explain a substantial fraction of the variance in excess noise levels across promoters (17%).
evidence: Statistical analysis of model fit to data

claim: The top five TFs most significantly associated with elevated noise levels of their targets were CRP, H-NS, ArcA, ilvY, and GadX.
source: The top five TFs most significantly associated with elevated noise levels of their targets were CRP, H-NS, ArcA, ilvY, and GadX (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Results from statistical analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: H-NS is a histone-like nucleoid-associated protein that acts as a silencer.
source: The appearance of H-NS is interesting since it is a histone-like nucleoid-associated protein that acts as a silencer (Dorman, 2004), that is, somewhat analogous to the role of nucleosomes in eukaryotes, and in eukaryotes nucleosome positioning at promoters has been shown to be a major determinant of transcriptional noise (Blake et al., 2006; Tirosh and Barkai, 2008; Cairns, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dorman, 2004 and studies on nucleosome positioning

claim: A substantial amount of variation in noise levels can be explained by noise-propagation from noisy regulators.
source: In summary, modeling of excess noise levels in terms of known regulatory interactions shows that, in accordance with our model, a substantial amount of the variation in noise levels can be explained by noise-propagation from noisy regulators, and the regulators we identify as most significantly propagating noise are consistent with existing biological knowledge regarding our growth conditions.
evidence: Conclusion from statistical modeling of experimental data

claim: Native promoters must have experienced selective pressures that increased their noise levels.
source: Here we have shown that, by comparing naturally observed variation in a particular trait with variation observed in synthetic systems that were evolved under well-controlled selective conditions, definite inferences can be made about the selection pressures that have acted on the natural systems. In particular, by evolving synthetic E. coli promoters de novo using a procedure in which promoters are strongly selected on their mean expression and not on their expression noise, we have shown that native promoters must have experienced selective pressures that increased their noise levels, and that promoters with elevated noise are highly regulated by TFs.
evidence: Conclusion from experimental observations and comparison between synthetic and native promoters

claim: Promoters with elevated noise are highly regulated by TFs.
source: In particular, by evolving synthetic E. coli promoters de novo using a procedure in which promoters are strongly selected on their mean expression and not on their expression noise, we have shown that native promoters must have experienced selective pressures that increased their noise levels, and that promoters with elevated noise are highly regulated by TFs.
evidence: Observed in experimental data shown in Figure 2

claim: Noise-propagation is often beneficial and can be considered to act as a rudimentary form of regulation.
source: Our model elucidates that not only the condition-response effect but also the noise-propagation effect is often a functional consequence of the regulatory interaction; that is, instead of being just an unavoidable side-effect of regulation, noise-propagation is often beneficial and can be considered to act as a rudimentary form of regulation.
evidence: Conclusion from theoretical model

claim: Noise-propagation alone may provide a sufficient benefit for a new regulatory interaction to evolve.
source: Our framework vastly expands the evolutionary conditions under which novel regulatory interactions can evolve. Instead of assuming that regulators and their targets must evolve in a tightly coordinated fashion, noise-propagation alone may provide a sufficient benefit for a new regulatory interaction to evolve.
evidence: Conclusion from theoretical model

claim: The theory provides a plausible scenario for how accurate regulatory interactions can evolve de novo from a state without regulation.
source: In this way our model provides a plausible scenario for how accurate regulatory interactions can evolve de novo from a state without regulation.
evidence: Conclusion from theoretical model

claim: Unless regulation is very precise, regulatory interactions that act to increase noise are beneficial.
source: Finally, our model shows that unless regulation is very precise, regulatory interactions that act to increase noise are beneficial.
evidence: Conclusion from theoretical model

claim: Elevated levels of expression noise can be expected whenever the accuracy of regulation is limited.
source: Thus, elevated levels of expression noise can be expected whenever the accuracy of regulation is limited.
evidence: Conclusion from theoretical model

claim: Random DNA sequences 100-150 base pairs in length were synthesized and cloned upstream of a strong ribosomal binding site and GFP open reading frame.
source: We synthesized a pool of random DNA sequences, 100–150 base pairs in length, and cloned these upstream of a sequence containing a strong ribosomal binding site and the open reading frame of green fluorescent protein (GFP).
evidence: Description of experimental methodology

claim: The fitness of promoter genotypes strongly depends on their mean μ and is almost independent of their excess noise.
source: This estimated fitness function indicated that the fitness of promoter genotypes strongly depends on their mean μ and is almost independent of their excess noise (Appendix 2—figure 3 and Appendix 2—figure 4).
evidence: Analysis of fitness function shown in Appendix 2 figures

claim: Applying additional rounds of selection of varying strengths to the population of evolved promoters did not systematically alter their distribution of excess noise levels.
source: In addition, applying additional rounds of selection of varying strengths to the population of evolved promoters did not systematically alter their distribution of excess noise levels.
evidence: Experimental observation from additional selection experiments

claim: Propagation of expression noise from regulators to their targets acts as a rudimentary form of regulation that facilitates the evolution of more accurate regulation.
source: The theory shows that propagation of expression noise from regulators to their targets is not an unwanted side-effect of regulation, but rather acts as a rudimentary form of regulation that facilitates the evolution of more accurate regulation.
evidence: Main conclusion from theoretical model presented in the study

claim: Contrary to expectations, promoters exhibit low noise by default.
source: By evolving synthetic Escherichia coli promoters de novo, we here show that, contrary to expectations, promoters exhibit low noise by default.
evidence: Main experimental finding from synthetic promoter evolution

claim: Selection must have acted to increase the noise levels of highly regulated E. coli promoters.
source: Instead, selection must have acted to increase the noise levels of highly regulated E. coli promoters.
evidence: Inference from comparison of synthetic and native promoters
